materials.title: 2010年 考研英语一 Reading Part A Text 1
materials.text:
Of all the changes that have taken place in English-language newspapers during the past quarter-century, perhaps the most far-reaching has been the inexorable decline in the scope and seriousness of their arts coverage.

It is difficult to the point of impossibility for the average reader under the age of forty to imagine a time when high-quality arts criticism could be found in most big-city newspapers. Yet a considerable number of the most significant collections of criticism published in the 20th century consisted in large part of newspaper reviews. To read such books today is to marvel at the fact that their learned contents were once deemed suitable for publication in general-circulation dailies.

We are even farther removed from the unfocused newspaper reviews published in England between the turn of the 20th century and the eve of World War II, at a time when newsprint was dirt-cheap and stylish arts criticism was considered an ornament to the publications in which it appeared. In those far-off days, it was taken for granted that the critics of major papers would write in detail and at length about the events they covered. Theirs was a serious business, and even those reviewers who wore their learning lightly, like George Bernard Shaw and Ernest Newman, could be trusted to know what they were about. These men believed in journalism as a calling, and were proud to be published in the daily press.

Unfortunately, these critics are virtually forgotten. Neville Cardus, who wrote for the Manchester Guardian from 1917 until shortly before his death in 1975, is now known solely as a writer of essays on the game of cricket. During his lifetime, though, he was also one of England's foremost classical-music critics. He was knighted in 1967, the first music critic to be so honored. Yet only one of his books is now in print, and his vast body of writings on music is unknown save to specialists.

Is there any chance that Cardus's criticism will enjoy a revival? The prospect seems remote. Journalistic tastes had changed long before his death, and postmodern readers have little use for the richly upholstered prose in which he specialized. Moreover, the amateur tradition in music criticism has been in headlong retreat.

materials.title: 2010年 考研英语一 Reading Part A Text 2
materials.text:
Over the past decade, thousands of patents have been granted for what are called business methods. Amazon.com received one for its "one-click" online payment system. Merrill Lynch got legal protection for an asset allocation strategy. One inventor patented a technique for lifting a box.

Now the nation's top patent court appears completely ready to scale back on business-method patents, which have been controversial ever since they were first authorized 10 years ago. In a move that has intellectual-property lawyers abuzz, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit said it would use a particular case to conduct a broad review of business-method patents. In re Bilski, as the case is known, is "a very big deal," says Dennis D. Crouch of the University of Missouri School of Law. It "has the potential to eliminate an entire class of patents."

Curbs on business-method claims would be a dramatic about-face, because it was the Federal Circuit itself that introduced such patents with its 1998 decision in the so-called State Street Bank case, approving a patent on a way of pooling mutual-fund assets. That ruling produced an explosion in business-method filings, initially by emerging internet companies trying to stake out exclusive rights to specific types of online transactions. Later, more established companies raced to add such patents to their files, if only as a defensive move against rivals that might beat them to the punch.

The Bilski case involves a claimed patent on a method for hedging risk in the commodities market. The Federal Circuit issued an unusual order stating that the case would be heard by all 12 of the court's judges, rather than a typical panel of three, and that one issue it wants to evaluate is whether it should "reconsider" its State Street Bank ruling.

materials.title: 2010年 考研英语一 Reading Part A Text 3
materials.text:
In his book The Tipping Point, Malcolm Gladwell argues that social epidemics are driven in large part by the actions of a tiny minority of special individuals, often called influentials, who are unusually informed, persuasive, or well-connected. The idea is intuitively compelling, but it doesn't explain how ideas actually spread.

The supposed importance of influentials derives from a plausible-sounding but largely untested theory called the "two-step flow of communication": information flows from the media to the influentials and from them to everyone else. Marketers have embraced the two-step flow because it suggests that if they can just find and influence the influentials, those select people will do most of the work for them. The theory also seems to explain the sudden and unexpected popularity of certain looks, brands, or neighborhoods.

In recent years, however, researchers have begun to test the hypothesis using computer simulations and empirical studies of online networks. They have found that outside of a few special cases, the global cascade of a trend depends far less on a handful of super-connectors than on the critical mass of easily influenced ordinary people interacting with one another.

Some researchers argue that <u>these people</u> are often misled by their own retrospective bias: when a trend catches fire, observers naturally point to prominent early adopters and assume those individuals caused the cascade, ignoring the thousands of ordinary transmitters who actually sustained the chain reaction.

materials.title: 2010年 考研英语一 Reading Part A Text 4
materials.text:
Bankers have been blaming themselves for their troubles in public. Behind the scenes, they have been taking aim at someone else: the accounting standard-setters. Their rules, moan the banks, have forced them to report enormous losses, and it's just not fair. These rules say they must value some assets at the price a third party would pay, not the price managers think they are worth.

Unfortunately for the lobbyists, the politicians who were once sympathetic to the banks' complaints have begun to realize that shooting the messenger does not cure the disease. Fair-value accounting (also known as mark-to-market) did not cause the financial crisis; it merely exposed the scale of reckless lending earlier than traditional historical-cost accounting would have done.

Under the old regime, banks could carry troubled loans at their original face value until a borrower formally defaulted, allowing executives to conceal deteriorating balance sheets for years. When standard-setters tightened the rules, they sought to give investors a transparent, timely snapshot of financial health.

While some tweaks to fair-value rules may be justified for truly illiquid assets during extreme market freezes, gutting the standards to flatter bank earnings would only prolong investor distrust and delay economic recovery.

materials.text:
One basic weakness in a conservation system based wholly on economic motives is that most members of the land community have no economic value. (46) <u>Scientists have painfully learned that the ecological balance of an environment is maintained by the complex interaction of all its plant and animal species, regardless of whether humans find them commercially useful.</u> Yet when an economist or a policymaker evaluates a natural habitat, species without direct market value are routinely treated as dispensable.

When one non-commercial species is threatened with extinction, conservationists are often forced to invent an economic excuse to save it. (47) <u>We tend to manufacture superficial financial arguments for preserving wildflowers or songbirds, so that their survival can be justified in the language of profit and loss.</u> Such excuses are rarely convincing, and they leave the majority of wild species unprotected.

Some biologists have recently discovered that certain obscure insects and fungi play a measurable role in maintaining soil fertility for timber trees. (48) <u>However, a conservation policy driven solely by short-term economic self-interest tends to ignore, and thus eventually to eliminate, many elements of the land community that lack the commercial value to pay their own way.</u>

In Europe and North America, governments have increasingly stepped in to fund wildlife refuges and reforestation programs. (49) <u>This public intervention is carried out on the assumption that the state must perform vital ecological tasks that private landowners would not be done for their own financial gain.</u>

Ultimately, however, government agencies cannot police every acre of forest, wetland, and prairie. (50) <u>An ethical obligation on the part of the private owner is the only visible remedy for these situations, since healthy ecosystems depend on daily stewardship that no law can fully enforce.</u>
